question: to the Commission Raphaël Glucksmann (S&D), Kathleen Van Brempt (S&D), Klára Dobrev (S&D) Subject:

According to an investigation published on 31 March 2026 by The World (PRX), the NGO China Labor Watch interviewed 50 Chinese migrant workers at the BYD factory construction site in Szeged, Hungary. Workers reportedly faced seven-day working weeks, 14-hour days, non-payment of overtime, the withholding of 20–30 % of their wages, and recruitment fees constituting debt bondage. A local labour authority investigation is reportedly under way. These allegations follow findings by Brazil’s Ministry of Labour and Employment of similar violations at a BYD construction site in Camaçari, where investigators accused the company and its contractors of trafficking migrant workers into conditions analogous to slavery. 1.
Is the Commission aware of these allegations, and what action has it taken to date?

Does it have information on other cases within the EU where non-EU companies have imported workers from their country of origin and exercise coercive control over them? Has the European Labour Authority been involved or offered support in this case or in similar cases?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to investigate the alleged violations in Szeged and prevent such practices across the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) The co-legislators have adopted legislation inter alia to strengthen the enforcement of fundamental rights in supply chains, in particular the Forced Labour Regulation1 and the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive2. The Commission is working on their implementation to ensure that level playing field and fundamental rights are respected throughout supply chains. The Commission is aware of the allegations on labour rights violations at the BYD factory construction site in Szeged, Hungary. According to the Commission’s information, there is a case pending before the Hungarian Labour Inspectorate related to the allegations. The Hungarian Labour Inspectorate is the competent authority to investigate this matter. The Commission does not interfere in cases pending before the competent national authorities. The Commission informed the European Labour Authority (ELA) of the concerns in Hungary’s electric vehicle supply chain. ELA invited the Hungarian authorities to examine the matter offering ELA’s support, given ELA does not have investigative powers.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2024 on

prohibiting products made with forced labour on the Union market and amending Directive (EU) 2019/1937 (Text with EEA relevance), OJ L, 2024/3015, 12.12.2024 - https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/3015/oj/eng. 2 Directive (EU) of the European Parliament 2024/1760 and of the Council of 13 June 2024 on corporate sustainability due diligence and amending Directive (EU) 2019/1937 - https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1760/oj/eng and Regulation (EU) 2023/2859 (Text with EEA relevance) - https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2859/oj/eng.
